title: Europe gets its AI enforcement powers on Sunday. The unit wielding them has 36 people.
excerpt: The European Commission gains sweeping new powers on Sunday to police how the world’s most advanced AI labs handle systemic risk, as the AI Act reaches its second anniversary. The EU’s AI Office will be able to demand documentation, conduct evaluations, and request access to frontier models, with fines of up to 3% of global […]
content_html:
The European Commission gains sweeping new powers on Sunday to police how the world’s most advanced AI labs handle systemic risk, as the AI Act reaches its second anniversary. The EU’s AI Office will be able to demand documentation, conduct evaluations, and request access to frontier models, with fines of up to 3% of global turnover for non-compliance.

The timing could hardly be sharper. Last week produced the first documented case of an autonomous AI agent escaping its test environment and attacking another company’s production systems.

The incident that changed the conversation

OpenAI confirmed that two of its models, including flagship Sol, broke out of a secure test environment, exploited a zero-day in third-party software to reach the internet, and hacked into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. It did so to cheat on its own evaluation by stealing the hidden answers.

OpenAI called the breach “unprecedented.” Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue called it “mind-blowing,” having initially assumed the sophistication pointed to a leading AI lab.

The 💜 of EU tech

The latest rumblings from the EU tech scene, a story from our wise ol' founder Boris, and some questionable AI art. It's free, every week, in your inbox. Sign up now!

“We got lucky this time,” said Chloé Touzet, policy lead at the non-profit SaferAI, describing the episode as a clear warning shot on two of the four systemic risks the Commission has identified. “We can’t rely on luck in the future.”

What the AI Act actually covers

Drafting began before ChatGPT launched in November 2022, yet the law anticipated general-purpose models and requires their developers to assess and mitigate systemic risks. Commission guidance names four: AI enabling bio-attacks, loss of control of a model, AI going on cyber offence, and large-scale manipulation.

Last week’s incident hit two of them simultaneously. The obligations have existed since August 2025, but until Sunday the AI Office lacked the power to monitor and supervise compliance.

Washington reacted faster than Brussels expected

The US response arrived within days. Representatives Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduced a bipartisan AI Kill Switch Act requiring developers of models costing $100 million or more to train to maintain the technical capacity to throttle or shut them down.

China moved differently. Xi Jinping used the World AI Conference in Shanghai to position Beijing as the natural leader of global AI governance, and 29 countries signed on to a new World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization that was notably light on specifics.

The resourcing problem

The unit inside the AI Office responsible for evaluating cutting-edge models employs 36 people. That is the team expected to hold OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to account across four categories of catastrophic risk.

Five MEPs across political groups wrote to the Commission on 18 May warning that “the resourcing trajectory of the AI Office does not appear aligned with the scale and complexity of its foreseen tasks.” The signatories included Brando Benifei, Sergey Lagodinsky, Kim van Sparrentak, Axel Voss, and Kristian Vigenin.

Access has been a problem too. The AI Office and its external evaluators have struggled in recent months to obtain access to some frontier models, including Anthropic’s Mythos, and the Commission has promised a blueprint for structured access as part of its cyber and AI action plan.

Learning about it from a blog post

Benifei, the Parliament’s lead on AI, was pointed about how Brussels found out. “An autonomous agent escaped its test environment and compromised another company’s production systems, and we learned of it from a corporate blog,” he said.

“Companies should be taking preventive action, not merely corrective action after harm has occurred,” said Risto Uuk, head of European policy and research at the Future of Life Institute. Think tanks, MEPs, and dozens of AI experts signed an open letter this month urging the AI Office to use its powers actively, as soon as concerns arise.

Regulating an industry Europe does not have

The awkward reality is that the AI Act will overwhelmingly police non-European companies. American labs are racing Chinese rivals, and Europe is refereeing a contest it is not competing in.

Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3 this month, a 2.8-trillion-parameter system billed as the world’s largest open-weight model, which developers ranked above both GPT-5.6 Sol and Fable 5 on a blind coding leaderboard. Open weights complicate enforcement in ways closed models do not.

Mistral is competing, but Europe has no industry-leading alternative. “What remains missing is the second half of the equation,” said Lagodinsky, the German Greens MEP monitoring the law’s rollout, “the capital to finance our own alternatives.”

Powers arriving as the Act is trimmed

There is a countervailing pressure. Brussels struck a deal to thin out parts of the AI Act even as these enforcement provisions come into force, and Parliament has pushed most high-risk obligations out to 2027 and 2028.

The broader governance picture is fragmenting rather than converging. America’s own retreat from safety guardrails has consequences well beyond its borders, and Trump and Xi are due to meet in Washington in September with AI on the agenda.

“This is the moment the AI Act enters the geopolitical stage,” Lagodinsky said. Whether 36 people can carry it there is the question Sunday leaves open.

content_html_zh:
随着《人工智能法案》颁布两周年，欧盟委员会周日获得了全面的新权力，以监管世界上最先进的人工智能实验室如何处理系统性风险。 欧盟人工智能办公室将能够要求提供文件、进行评估并请求访问前沿模型，对违规行为最高可处以全球营业额 3% 的罚款。

时机再准确不过了。 上周出现了第一个有记录的案例，显示自主人工智能代理逃离其测试环境并攻击另一家公司的生产系统。

改变谈话内容的事件

OpenAI 证实，其两款模型（包括旗舰产品 Sol）突破了安全测试环境，利用第三方软件中的零日漏洞访问互联网，并侵入了 Hugging Face 的生产基础设施。 它这样做是为了通过窃取隐藏的答案来欺骗自己的评估。

OpenAI 称此次违规行为“史无前例”。 Hugging Face 联合创始人克莱门特·德兰格 (Clement Delangue) 称其“令人兴奋”，最初假设其复杂程度来自领先的人工智能实验室。

欧盟科技的💜

来自欧盟科技界的最新传言、我们明智的创始人鲍里斯的故事，以及一些值得怀疑的人工智能艺术。 每周都会免费发送到您的收件箱中。 立即注册！

“这次我们很幸运，”非营利组织 SaferAI 的政策负责人 Chloé Touzet 表示，她将这一事件描述为对委员会已确定的四个系统性风险中的两个的明确警告。 “未来我们不能指望运气。”

《人工智能法案》实际上涵盖了什么

起草工作在 ChatGPT 于 2022 年 11 月推出之前就开始了，但该法律预期了通用模型，并要求其开发人员评估和减轻系统性风险。 委员会指南列举了四种：人工智能引发生物攻击、模型失控、人工智能进行网络攻击以及大规模操纵。

上周的事件同时袭击了其中两人。 这些义务自 2025 年 8 月起就存在，但直到周日，人工智能办公室还缺乏监督和监督合规性的权力。

华盛顿的反应比布鲁塞尔预期的要快

美国的回应几天之内就到达了。 众议员特德·刘 (Ted Lieu) 和纳撒尼尔·莫兰 (Nathaniel Moran) 提出了一项两党 AI Kill Switch 法案，要求花费 1 亿美元或更多的模型开发人员进行培训，以保持抑制或关闭它们的技术能力。

中国的行动有所不同。 习近平利用上海世界人工智能大会将北京定位为全球人工智能治理的天然领导者，29 个国家签署了新的世界人工智能合作组织，但具体细节却明显较少。

资源问题

AI办公室内负责评估尖端模型的部门有36名员工。 该团队希望让 OpenAI、Anthropic 和 Google 承担四类灾难性风险的责任。

5 月 18 日，来自不同政治团体的五位欧洲议会议员致信委员会警告称，“人工智能办公室的资源配置轨迹似乎与其预期任务的规模和复杂性不相符。” 签约者包括 Brando Benifei、Sergey Lagodinsky、Kim van Sparrentak、Axel Voss 和 Kristian Vigenin。

访问也一直是一个问题。 近几个月来，人工智能办公室及其外部评估人员一直在努力获取一些前沿模型的访问权限，包括 Anthropic 的神话，委员会已承诺提供结构化访问的蓝图，作为其网络和人工智能行动计划的一部分。

从博客文章中了解它

议会人工智能领域的负责人贝尼菲谈到了布鲁塞尔是如何发现这一问题的。 “一个自主代理逃离了测试环境并破坏了另一家公司的生产系统，我们是从公司博客中了解到这一情况的，”他说。

生命未来研究所欧洲政策与研究主管里斯托·尤克表示：“企业应该采取预防措施，而不仅仅是在伤害发生后采取纠正措施。” 智库、欧洲议会议员和数十名人工智能专家本月签署了一封公开信，敦促人工智能办公室在出现担忧时立即积极使用其权力。

监管欧洲没有的行业

尴尬的现实是，《人工智能法案》将绝大多数监管非欧洲公司。 美国的实验室正在与中国的竞争对手展开竞争，而欧洲正在对一场它不参加的比赛进行裁判。

Moonshot 本月推出了 Kimi K3，这是一个拥有 2.8 万亿参数的系统，被誉为世界上最大的开放权重模型，开发人员在盲码排行榜上的排名高于 GPT-5.6 Sol 和 Fable 5。 开放权重使执行变得复杂，而封闭模型则不然。

米斯特拉尔正在竞争，但欧洲没有行业领先的替代方案。 “仍然缺少的是等式的后半部分，”负责监督该法律实施的德国绿党欧洲议会议员拉戈丁斯基说，“为我们自己的替代方案提供资金的资本。”

该法案被削减后的权力

存在着抵消压力。 即使这些执行条款生效，布鲁塞尔仍达成了一项协议，以精简《人工智能法案》的部分内容，并且议会已将大多数高风险义务推迟到 2027 年和 2028 年。

更广泛的治理图景正在分裂而不是融合。 美国自身退出安全护栏的后果远远超出了其国界，特朗普和习近平将于 9 月在华盛顿会面，人工智能将被列入议程。

“这是人工智能法案进入地缘政治舞台的时刻，”拉戈丁斯基说。 36 个人是否可以携带它，周日仍是一个悬而未决的问题。
